hints: Notice the contrast in the stem: most $\alpha$-particles pass straight through while a very small proportion rebound by more than $90^{\circ}$ toward the source.
Connect charge and mass to motion: $\alpha$-particles are positively charged and massive, so large-angle scattering needs a concentrated charge and a concentrated mass to push them back.
Ask for each conclusion whether the passing-through and rebounding observations alone distinguish it - especially whether scattering can identify different particles inside the nucleus.
walkthrough: Identify the evidence: most $\alpha$-particles pass through the gold foil undeflected, while about 1 in 8000 is scattered by more than $90^{\circ}$.
Most passing straight through means the atom is mainly empty space where the $\alpha$-particle experiences negligible force, supporting the empty-space conclusion.
Rebound through more than $90^{\circ}$ means the $\alpha$-particle hits something that can reverse its momentum, so that object must contain most of the atomic mass in a very small volume.
Because the $\alpha$-particle has charge $+2e$, its deflection must be due to electrostatic repulsion, so that small massive centre must be charged.

Nothing in straight-through transmission or back-scattering tells whether that charged mass is made of two types of nucleon, since neutrons were identified by later experiments. So the proton-plus-neutron composition cannot be drawn from this experiment alone. This is option C.

options.A: Most $\alpha$-particles go straight through, so they meet no obstacle in most of the atomic volume, which does support empty space.
options.B: Rebound of a heavy $\alpha$-particle through more than $90^{\circ}$ needs a direct hit on a much heavier object, which does support mass concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
options.C: Scattering shows a small, massive, charged nucleus exists, but gives no evidence about separate protons and neutrons inside it.
options.D: Deflection of positively charged $\alpha$-particles by electrostatic repulsion does support a concentrated positive charge in the nucleus.
